newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ministers agree to ban rearing calves in crates.
newsitem.headline: Ministers agree to ban rearing calves in crates.

text.p: European Union farm ministers agreed on Tuesday to improve the diet of young cows and to ban by 2006 the use of cramped crates for rearing calves over two months old, EU officials said.
New-style crates, already condemned by animal welfare groups as cruel, will be banned from January 1998 and old crates they were meant to replace phased out over eight years.

"This was a very important breakthrough on a contentious dossier where there were clearly great differences between producers and consumers," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates told a news conference after a two-day meeting.
Yates clinched a hard-won agreement crowning the six-month Irish EU Presidency after proposing a compromise which won over France, the EU's main user of veal crates.

France obtained a pledge that the European Commission would examine any trade distortion caused by a new early marketing subsidy scheme for calves which angry French farmers said favoured their Dutch competitors.
In the end only Italy voted against and Spain abstained.
France, Italy and the Netherlands account for most of the six million veal calves reared annually in the EU.
Britain, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Austria and Finland, who pressed for a veal crate ban, succeeded in reducing the phasing out period by two years from the 10 initially planned.
A Commission report said calves suffer severe stress and health problems when they are confined in individual crates and fed on a milky diet lacking iron in order to produce white meat.
Calves will now be given a minimum daily ration of hay and other fibres while those kept in group pens will be given more room to move.
Calves weighing less than 150 kg must each have at least 1.5 square metres space to move while those over 220 kg must have at least 1.8 square metres.
Farmers may receive EU aid to adjust to the new production rules.
